title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking & runbooks
author: Evelyn Cho
body:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team ownership for the Redwood Inference serving runtime. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers onboarding to the runtime, oncall SREs, and performance-focused contributors.

Goals and scope
- Provide a single source of truth combining architecture and operations for the runtime.
- Document kernel scheduling heuristics and configuration knobs.
- Provide reproducible profiling and benchmarking steps and CI integrations.
- Surface known issues and mitigation paths.
- Provide runbooks for common incidents and day-2 ops.

High-level architecture (summary)

The serving runtime implements a two-layer architecture:
1) Inference runtime (per-node): GPU-optimized inference engine that manages model weights, KV cache, batching, and kernel selection.
2) Orchestration layer (control plane): fleet management, routing policies, autoscaling, and rollout control.

Key components
- runtime-agent: local process on each GPU host that manages model containers, health checks, and telemetry exports.
- kernel-selector: library used by the runtime to select CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN/TVM kernels and quantized execution paths at load time and dynamically at runtime.
- batch-scheduler: continuous-batching component with latency-first and throughput-first modes.
- kv-cache-service: local in-memory cache for key/value attention caches and prefix caching.
- telemetry-exporter: Prometheus/OpenTelemetry exporter for per-token and per-request metrics.

SLOs and operational targets
- 99th percentile latency for standard text-generation (seq_len=256, batch=1): <= 120 ms (p99).
- 95th percentile latency for chat (avg seq_len=128): <= 85 ms (p95).
- Median tokens/sec for throughput workloads (batching enabled, 8x A100): >= 14k tokens/sec per GPU for gpt-6.7B-like models.
- Error rate (5xx) target: < 0.1% sustained.

Kernel scheduling design

Overview
The kernel scheduler chooses the best execution path for each operator (attention, matmul, softmax, layernorm) based on: model architecture, dtypes (fp16, bf16, int8), sequence length distribution, batch size, and GPU type. Kernel selection happens at two times:
- Model load / AOT: choose a baseline kernel set for the expected workload.
- Runtime switch: monitor latencies and switch to alternate kernels if p99 or hardware counters indicate regressions.

Selection heuristics
- If sequence_length > 1024 and model supports tiled-attention kernel, prefer tiled kernel.
- For int8 quantized profiles, prefer int8 GEMM kernels with accumulator strategies; fallback to fp16 if accuracy checks fail on canary runs.
- Use GPU-specific path for A100 vs H100 (use tensor core tiling parameters tuned per-device).

Config knobs (examples)
| setting_key | description | default | valid_values |
| REDWOOD_KERNEL_SELECTOR_MODE | Kernel selection policy | safety-first | safety-first, latency-first, throughput-first |
| MAX_BATCH_SIZE | Max in-flight batch size | 32 | integer |
| KERNEL_RETRAIN_THRESHOLD | Metric delta (%) to trigger dynamic switch | 10 | integer percentage |

Runtime fallback and safety
- All dynamic kernel switches require: (a) preflight micro-benchmark against a small prompt set, (b) accuracy check (rounded-k-L2) if quantized, and (c) feature-compatible fallback (e.g., nv-merge disabled).
- On mismatch or increased errors, runtime will revert to last-known-good kernel set and emit event to /events/runtime/kernel-fallback.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

Purpose: produce deterministic profiles to diagnose latency spikes, kernel stalls, and memory pressure.
Prerequisites: access to host (ssh to gpu-host-<id>), root or runtime-admin, Docker / containerd access, and profiling tools (Nsight Systems, Nsight Compute, perf, pprof).

1) Collect lightweight runtime metrics
- Check Prometheus metrics: curl http://metrics:9090/metrics | grep runtime_ or use Grafana dashboard 'runtime/perf'.
- Identify time window of spike and retrieve trace_id or request_id.

2) Reproduce with local workload
- Use benchmark harness: tools/bench/run_local_load.py --model gpt-6.7B --seq 256 --batch 1 --qps 50 --target-host gpu-host-12
- If reproducing in container: docker exec -it runtime-container /bin/bash and run harness inside the container.

3) System-level profiling (short run)
- Nsight Systems (recommended for overall flows):
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --output=profile1 --duration 30s \\
    python tools/bench/run_local_load.py --model gpt-6.7B --seq 256 --batch 1 --target-host localhost
- Collect the .qdrep and open in Nsight GUI or use nsys stats for quick checks.

4) Kernel-level profiling (deeper)
- Nsight Compute (for specific kernels):
  ncu --target-processes all --set full --kernel-id ::curl
  # recommended: run a 10s sample capturing top matmul/attention kernels
- Check per-kernel SASS time, register spill, and memory throughput.

5) CPU-side flamegraphs and pprof
- Enable pprof endpoint: curl http://localhost:8080/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 > cpu.pprof
- Convert to flamegraph: go tool pprof -http=:6060 ./binary cpu.pprof

6) Memory and NVLink checks
- nvml-smi dmon and nvidia-smi topo -m for connectivity; watch for PCIe vs NVLink fallbacks.

7) Telemetry correlation
- Correlate request-id and trace_id via distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry). Use Jaeger to inspect spans and duration breakdowns.

Benchmarking suite (reproducible tests)

Bench principles
- Benchmarks are deterministic: fixed seed, fixed prompt set, controlled concurrency.
- Tests include: latency p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, mem-usage, and batch scaling curve.
- Bench harness lives in repo: experiments/benchmarks/serving-suite. CI job: bench/ci/serving-bench.

Standard test cases
- micro-latency: seq_len=128, batch=1, 1000 requests at 10 qps
- long-context: seq_len=2048, batch=1, 200 requests at 2 qps
- throughput-scale: seq_len=256, batch sweep [1,2,4,8,16,32] to measure tokens/sec and GPU utilization
- quantized-accuracy: int8 profile vs fp16 baseline across 500 eval prompts, report BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics and L2 error per token

CI integration
- Bench runs tagged with git commit and model-version. Results stored in BenchDB (S3) at s3://redwood-bench/serving/YYYY-MM-DD/<commit>.csv
- Regression alert rule: any p95 increase > 8% or tokens/sec drop > 10% triggers bench-alert channel and opens a regression ticket.

Release notes (recent)
- 2026-02-20 (v2.14.0): Improved kernel-selection heuristics for H100 (tile size auto-tune), reduced p99 latency by median 12% on gpt-6.7B; added telemetry for kernel-switch events; fixed cache eviction bug (runtime #4217).
- 2025-12-05 (v2.12.3): Backported int8 stability patches and added canary quantized-accuracy checks in load path.

Known issues (tracked)
- ISSUE-8342: Intermittent p99 spikes when NVLink topology changes (symptom: repeated remaps in nvidia-smi). Workaround: restart runtime-agent on the host to reinitialize topology cache. Owner: eng-infra.
- ISSUE-7980: Quantized int8 path sometimes produces token-level L2 > 1e-3 on small vocab models. Workaround: use fp16 profile until per-model tuning is complete. Owner: applied-ml.
- ISSUE-9101: Under high concurrency (>= 600 in-flight requests) batch-scheduler may exceed GPU memory estimates causing OOM. Mitigation: reduce MAX_BATCH_SIZE or enable preemptive eviction (config key PREEMPTIVE_EVICTION). Owner: eng-serving-runtime.

Runbooks (incidents and common ops)

Runbook: High p99 latency for production route
1) Identify scope: query Grafana panel (route:prod-llm) and find affected hosts.
2) Check recent kernel-switch events: curl http://<host>:9100/events | jq '.events[] | select(.type=="kernel-switch")'
3) If kernel-switch occurred within window: revert dynamic switches by setting REDWOOD_KERNEL_SELECTOR_MODE=safety-first and restart runtime-agent: sudo systemctl restart runtime-agent
4) If no kernel-switch: profile short window with nsys (see profiling playbook) and inspect GPU utilization.
5) If OOMs present: check dmesg and container logs; scale out by adding nodes to the job via orchestration console and reduce MAX_BATCH_SIZE for affected model.
6) Post-incident: run benchmark suite against affected model and open a regression ticket with bench artifacts attached.

Runbook: Node-level OOM / GPU OOMs
1) Evacuate in-flight traffic: change routing policy to failover region or lower tier.
2) Collect memory stats: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv
3) Restart runtime-container if necessary: docker restart <container>
4) If persistent: mark node for maintenance in fleet manager, and trigger hardware checks.

Team wiki and ownership
- primary owners: eng-serving-runtime (oncall: @runtime-oncall slack).
- rotation: 2-week oncall rotation, ROTA in /teams/eng-serving-runtime/rotation.md.
- escalation: pager to SRE after 15 minutes if incident not acknowledged.

Appendix: useful commands and config snippets
- Dump kernel selection plan for model:
  curl http://localhost:8080/debug/kernel-plan?model=gpt-6.7B
- Quick fallback switch (ephemeral):
  export REDWOOD_KERNEL_SELECTOR_MODE=safety-first
  sudo systemctl restart runtime-agent

- Example kernel selector config (yaml):
  kernel_selector_mode: latency-first
  max_batch_size: 32
  quant_profiles:
    - name: int8_mixed
      accuracy_threshold: 0.999

References and related docs
- experiments/benchmarks/serving-suite (repo)
- eng-serving-runtime/runbooks (team wiki)
- observability-standards (confluence)
- incident-review/ISSUE-8342 (detailed analysis)

Document change log
- 2025-11-12: initial draft (Evelyn Cho).
- 2026-02-28: expanded profiling playbook, added H100 kernel heuristics, updated release notes.

If you cannot reproduce an issue using the steps above or need privileged access for profiling tools, contact the runtime owners (@runtime-oncall) or open a ticket in #runtime-ticketing.
